sections.title: 1. Framing the Question: Corruption vs. Ordering (Slide 3)
sections.description: What we are protecting against and the single-core assumption used to analyze Slides 5–16.

blocks.title: What Are We Protecting Against? (Slide 3)
blocks.content:
In `PCO_3_sectioncritique.pdf` (Slide 3), we ask a precise question:

> *Quand est-il nécessaire de garantir l'exclusion mutuelle sur l'accès à une variable globale ?*

To analyze the **12 concrete C++ scenarios (Slides 5–16)** cleanly, the course makes two explicit framing choices:

1. **Data Corruption / Broken Behavior vs. Instruction Ordering:**
   * We do **not** care about *instruction ordering* (*la séquentialité des instructions* — i.e., whether `TacheA` happens to run before `TacheB` or vice versa). In concurrent programming, different valid schedules naturally produce different orderings.
   * We **do** care about **not corrupting data or program behavior** (*ne pas corrompre des données ou le fonctionnement*): torn values, lost updates, lost assignments, or inconsistent multi-field states that could *never* occur in any sequential execution.
2. **The Single-Core Assumption (*processeur simple cœur*):**
   * Slides 5–16 assume a **32-bit single-core CPU** with **1 shared L1 cache**.
   * Only one task executes at any instant; a context switch (preemption) can **only** happen **between** individual machine instructions, never in the middle of one.
   * Why start here? Because any scenario that **already breaks on a single core** is guaranteed to be broken everywhere—and as Slide 17 will show, even scenarios that look "safe" on a single core break on **multi-core** hardware!

sections.description: Why Slide 13 is UNSAFE (unlike Slide 10), architecture-dependent floats/doubles, and std::vector<bool> bit-packing.

blocks.title: Slide 13: `var++` vs. `var = b` — UNSAFE! (Lost Assignment)
blocks.content:
### Slide 13 — One Increment, One Assignment (`var++` vs. `var = b`)
```cpp
static int var;

void TacheA() { ... var++; ... }
void TacheB() { int b; ... var = b; ... }
```
* **Single-Core Verdict:** **UNSAFE** (Needs mutual exclusion!)
* **Why (Do NOT confuse with Slide 10!):** In Slide 10, `taskB` only *read* `var` (`b = var`). Here, `TacheB` **writes** `var = b`! Trace this interleaving starting with `var = 5` and `b = 100`:
  1. `TacheA` executes `load var` into register `R0` (`R0 = 5`).
  2. **Context switch!** `TacheB` executes `var = b` (`var` becomes `100`).
  3. `TacheA` resumes with its stale `R0 = 5`, computes `R0 + 1 = 6`, and stores `var = 6`!
* **Result:** `TacheB`'s assignment (`100`) is **completely lost**! `var` ends up as `6`, which is neither `100` nor `101`—corrupting program behavior.

blocks.title: Master Reference: All 12 Scenarios (32-Bit Single-Core)
blocks.content:
| Slide | Code Pattern | 32-bit Single-Core Verdict | Primary Reason |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :--- |
| **5** | `var = a` / `var = b` (`int`) | **SAFE** | Single aligned 32-bit store instruction |
| **6** | `var = a` / `b = var` (`int`) | **SAFE** | Single store + single load |
| **7** | `var.a = a; var.b = b;` (×2) | **UNSAFE** | Two stores -> **torn struct** |
| **8** | `var.a = a; var.b = b;` / `a = var.a; b = var.b;` | **UNSAFE** | 1 writer + 1 reader still sees **torn struct** |
| **9** | `var++` / `var++` | **UNSAFE** | RMW (`load-add-store`) -> **lost update** |
| **10** | `var++` / `b = var` | **SAFE** | Reader does 1 load, never writes `var` |
| **11** | `var++` / `var++` / `c = var` | **UNSAFE** | Two `var++` tasks lose updates |
| **12** | `var++` / `b=var; if(b>10) var=0; else var++;` / `c=var` | **UNSAFE** | **Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU)** + concurrent `var++` |
| **13** | `var++` / `var = b` | **UNSAFE** | RMW + write -> **lost assignment** |
| **14** | `var = a` / `var = b` (`float`) | **SAFE** (32-bit) / **UNSAFE** (8/16-bit) | 32-bit `float` fits in 1 transfer on 32-bit CPU |
| **15** | `var = a` / `var = b` (`double`) | **UNSAFE** (32-bit) | 64-bit `double` takes two 32-bit stores -> **torn double** |
| **16** | `std::vector<bool>`: `vec[0] = a` / `vec[0] = b` (or `vec[1] = b`) | **UNSAFE** | Bit-packed byte RMW -> **clobbers adjacent bits** |

sections.title: 4. Single-Core vs. Multi-Core & The Golden Rule (Slide 17)
sections.description: Why single-core safety collapses on multi-core CPUs and why we must protect all concurrent accesses.

blocks.title: Single-Core vs. Multi-Core: Why Everything Changes
blocks.content:
Even the few scenarios marked **SAFE** on a 32-bit single-core CPU (Slides 5, 6, 10, 14) **cannot be left unprotected** in real systems. Slide 17 explains why:

| Dimension | Single-Core CPU (Slides 5–16) | Multi-Core CPU (Slide 17) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Execution** | Only 1 thread runs at a time; preemption happens *only between* machine instructions. | Multiple threads execute **simultaneously** on different cores. |
| **Caches** | **1 shared L1 cache** — every thread sees the same cache state immediately after an instruction. | Each core has **private L1/L2 caches** and **store buffers**. |
| **Synchronization** | Implicitly coherent for single-instruction aligned accesses. | *"Rien ne les oblige à synchroniser les caches si on ne le demande pas"* — cores may delay flushing or reading updates without memory barriers/mutexes. |
| **C++ Standard** | Compiler still assumes no data races! | Concurrent unsynchronized access (at least one write) is a **Data Race = Undefined Behavior (UB)** — the compiler may hoist loads out of loops or cache `var` in a register forever. |

> [!CAUTION]
> **The Golden Rule of PCO (Slide 17):**
> *"Dans le doute... **Protégez tous les accès concurrents !**"*
> (When in doubt, **protect all concurrent accesses**—with mutexes, semaphores, or `std::atomic`—which also emit the hardware memory barriers needed to synchronize multi-core caches!)

sections.title: 5. Active Recall: Flashcards, Reflection & Exam Quiz
sections.description: Test your mastery of all 12 scenarios, subtle traps, and multi-core cache coherency.

blocks.front:
32-bit Single-Core — Safe or Unsafe?

`taskA`: `var.a = a; var.b = b;`
`taskB`: `a = var.a; b = var.b;` (where `var` is `struct_t`)
blocks.back:
**UNSAFE!** (Slide 8)

Even with only 1 writer and 1 reader, reading two `int` fields takes two instructions. Preemption between `var.a` and `var.b` causes `taskB` to read a **torn struct** (old `a` + new `b`).
blocks.hint: Think about whether taskB reads both fields in one machine instruction.

blocks.front:
32-bit Single-Core — Safe or Unsafe?

Compare:
1) `var++` vs `b = var`
2) `var++` vs `var = b`
blocks.back:
1) `var++` vs `b = var` (Slide 10): **SAFE** — `b = var` is 1 load and never modifies `var`.
2) `var++` vs `var = b` (Slide 13): **UNSAFE!** — `TacheA` can load old `var`, get preempted while `TacheB` writes `var = b`, and overwrite `b` with `old_var + 1` (**lost assignment**).
blocks.hint: Which one modifies `var` while `var++` is mid-RMW?

blocks.front:
32-bit Single-Core — Safe or Unsafe?

`taskA`: `var++;`
`taskB`: `b = var; if (b > 10) var = 0; else var++;`
`taskC`: `c = var;`
blocks.back:
**UNSAFE!** (Slide 12)

1. **Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU):** `taskB` checks `b > 10`, gets preempted by `taskA` (`var++`), and then overwrites `var = 0` (losing `taskA`'s increment).
2. **Concurrent `var++`:** `taskB`'s `else` branch races with `taskA`'s `var++`.

blocks.front:
32-bit Single-Core — Safe or Unsafe?

1) `static float var;` (`var = a` / `var = b`)
2) `static double var;` (`var = a` / `var = b`)
blocks.back:
1) `float` (Slide 14): **SAFE on 32-bit/64-bit** (1 store), **UNSAFE on 8/16-bit MCUs**.
2) `double` (Slide 15): **UNSAFE on 32-bit** — a 64-bit `double` takes **two** 32-bit stores, risking a **torn `double`**.
blocks.hint: Compare the bit-width of `float` (32) and `double` (64) to a 32-bit CPU bus.

blocks.front:
32-bit Single-Core — Safe or Unsafe?

`std::vector<bool> vec;`
`TacheA`: `vec[0] = a;`
`TacheB`: `vec[1] = b;` (different indices!)
blocks.back:
**UNSAFE!** (Slide 16)

`std::vector<bool>` packs 8 booleans into **1 byte**. Writing `vec[0]` performs a non-atomic **read-modify-write** on the whole byte, clobbering `vec[1]`'s bit!
blocks.hint: How many bits does `std::vector<bool>` store per byte?

blocks.prompt: Explain why Slide 10 (`var++` vs. `b = var`) is SAFE against data corruption on a 32-bit single-core CPU, whereas Slide 13 (`var++` vs. `var = b`) is UNSAFE—and then explain why BOTH still require synchronization on a multi-core CPU.
self_check_criteria: Explains that in Slide 10, `b = var` is a single read-only `load` that never modifies `var`, so `var++` cannot lose an update.
Traces the Slide 13 interleaving (`TacheA` loads old `var` -> `TacheB` writes `var = b` -> `TacheA` stores `old + 1`), showing `TacheB`'s assignment is lost.
Explains multi-core hazards: private L1/L2 caches, store buffers, no automatic cache synchronization without barriers, and C++ Data Race Undefined Behavior (Slide 17).
blocks.model_answer: On a 32-bit single-core CPU, `var++` compiles to `load`, `add 1`, `store`. In Slide 10 (`var++` vs `b = var`), `taskB` only executes a single `load` instruction and never writes to `var`; even if `taskB` preempts `taskA` mid-`var++`, `taskB` gets a valid integer and `taskA` finishes its increment cleanly. In Slide 13 (`var++` vs `var = b`), `TacheA` can `load` the old `var`, get preempted while `TacheB` stores `var = b`, and then resume to store `old_var + 1`—completely losing `TacheB`'s assignment! Finally, on a multi-core CPU, both are unsafe without synchronization because each core has private L1/L2 caches (and store buffers) that are not forced to synchronize without explicit primitives (mutexes/atomics), and unsynchronized concurrent read+write is Undefined Behavior in C++ (Slide 17: 'Protégez tous les accès concurrents !').

blocks.question: In Slide 8, `taskA` writes `var.a = a; var.b = b;` and `taskB` only reads `a = var.a; b = var.b;` on a single-core CPU. Why is mutual exclusion STILL required?
options: Reading two fields takes two instructions, so `taskB` can be preempted mid-read and observe a torn struct (old `a` with new `b`).
Reading a `struct` always modifies its fields in memory.
Single-core CPUs cannot execute `taskB` while `taskA` exists.
Local variables `a` and `b` inside `taskB` are shared globally.
blocks.correct_answer: Reading two fields takes two instructions, so `taskB` can be preempted mid-read and observe a torn struct (old `a` with new `b`).
blocks.explanation: Even with 1 writer and 1 reader, `taskB` reads `var.a` and `var.b` in two separate instructions. If `taskA` updates both fields between `taskB`'s two reads, `taskB` gets an inconsistent half-old, half-new struct.
hints: Is reading two separate `int` fields atomic?
What happens if `taskA` runs between `a = var.a;` and `b = var.b;`?

blocks.question: Initially `var = 5` and `b = 100`. `TacheA` runs `var++;` and `TacheB` runs `var = b;` concurrently on a single-core CPU (Slide 13). Which final value of `var` proves data corruption / broken behavior?
options: `var == 6` (because `TacheA` loaded `5` before `TacheB` wrote `100`, then overwrote `100` with `6`).
`var == 100` (because `TacheA` finished `var++` before `TacheB` ran `var = 100`).
`var == 101` (because `TacheB` ran `var = 100` before `TacheA` ran `var++`).
None of the above — Slide 13 is safe on a single-core CPU.
blocks.correct_answer: `var == 6` (because `TacheA` loaded `5` before `TacheB` wrote `100`, then overwrote `100` with `6`).
blocks.explanation: `var == 100` and `var == 101` are valid sequential orderings. `var == 6` is impossible in any sequential execution: `TacheB`'s assignment `var = 100` was completely lost because `TacheA` was preempted after loading `5` and later stored `5 + 1 = 6`.
hints: Trace `TacheA` loading `var` into a register, getting preempted, and resuming after `TacheB` writes `100`.

blocks.question: In Slide 12, `taskB` executes `b = var; if (b > 10) var = 0; else var++;` while `taskA` executes `var++;`. What concurrency bug does `taskB` exhibit?
options: A Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU) race: `var` can change between `b = var` and `var = 0` (or `var++`).
Deadlock between `taskB` and `taskC`.
Stack overflow from `if (b > 10)`.
No bug, because `b` is a local variable.
blocks.correct_answer: A Check-Then-Act (TOCTOU) race: `var` can change between `b = var` and `var = 0` (or `var++`).
blocks.explanation: `taskB` checks a snapshot (`b = var`) and then acts on `var` later. `taskA` can modify `var` between the check and the write, causing lost increments or stale decisions.

blocks.question: Why can `static double var; var = a;` (executed concurrently by two threads, Slide 15) corrupt `var` on a 32-bit single-core CPU?
options: A 64-bit `double` requires two 32-bit memory writes, so a context switch between them produces a torn value.
Floating-point registers are shared across all threads in the same process.
C++ `double` variables are always stored on the stack, not in the data segment.
A `double` cannot be stored in a global variable.
blocks.correct_answer: A 64-bit `double` requires two 32-bit memory writes, so a context switch between them produces a torn value.
blocks.explanation: On a 32-bit architecture, writing a 64-bit `double` takes two separate 32-bit store instructions. If a preemption occurs between the first and second store, `var` ends up with 32 bits from Thread A and 32 bits from Thread B (a torn, corrupted floating-point value).
hints: How many bits wide is a `double` compared to a 32-bit CPU bus?
What happens if a context switch occurs halfway through writing a 64-bit value?

blocks.question: Why is concurrent modification of `std::vector<bool>` (Slide 16) dangerous even when Thread A only writes `vec[0]` and Thread B only writes `vec[1]`?
options: `std::vector<bool>` packs multiple booleans as bits inside the same byte, requiring a non-atomic read-modify-write of that byte.
`std::vector<bool>` allocates each boolean on a separate heap page.
`std::vector<bool>` is immutable after construction.
Each `bool` in `std::vector<bool>` is 64 bits wide.
blocks.correct_answer: `std::vector<bool>` packs multiple booleans as bits inside the same byte, requiring a non-atomic read-modify-write of that byte.
blocks.explanation: `std::vector<bool>` is a space-optimized specialization that stores 8 booleans per byte. Setting `vec[0]` reads the whole byte, flips bit 0, and writes the whole byte back—potentially overwriting Thread B's concurrent update to bit 1 (`vec[1]`).
hints: How does `std::vector<bool>` optimize memory usage in C++?
Can a CPU write a single bit in RAM without reading and writing the surrounding byte?

blocks.question: According to Slide 17, why is a simple `var = a` / `b = var` on `int` STILL unsafe without synchronization on a multi-core processor?
options: Each core has its own private cache (and store buffer), and nothing forces caches to synchronize without explicit synchronization operations (plus it is C++ Undefined Behavior).
Multi-core CPUs do not support the `int` data type.
Multi-core CPUs execute all threads on Core 0 only.
Context switches happen inside individual machine instructions on multi-core CPUs.
blocks.correct_answer: Each core has its own private cache (and store buffer), and nothing forces caches to synchronize without explicit synchronization operations (plus it is C++ Undefined Behavior).
blocks.explanation: On multi-core hardware, each core has private L1/L2 caches. Without mutexes, atomics, or memory barriers, updates may stay in a core's cache/store buffer unseen by other cores, and C++ treats unsynchronized concurrent read+write as Undefined Behavior. Hence the Golden Rule: 'Protégez tous les accès concurrents !'
hints: Recall Slide 17: 'Chaque cœur a sa propre mémoire cache...'
